name: Tragia
shared_traits: Small unisexual, petal-less flowers borne on racemes
Usually female flower(s) lower on the axis and male flowers above
look_here_first: Avoid touching the stinging plant. Photograph an intact reproductive raceme with scale, then examine leaf base, male-flower count and persistent pedicel stubs; confirm with mature capsule.

rows: Triangular-ovate serrate; truncate to cordate base
Variable; insufficient for a secure split
Short reproductive spike; inspect bracts and pedicels
Linear-lanceolate to narrowly ovate; truncate to weakly cordate

species_differences.leaf: Triangular-ovate serrate; truncate to cordate base
Variable; insufficient for a secure split
species_differences.raceme: 2–8(–10) staminate flowers; bracts 1–1.8 mm (FNA). Examine stigmatic surface and mature carpel count.
species_differences.pedicel: Persistent staminate pedicel base 0.4–1.5 mm (FNA); entirely overlaps T. ramosa, so not diagnostic alone.
species_differences.capsule: 6.5–7 mm wide (FNA); often only 1 of 3 carpels matures; capsule width overlaps T. ramosa (6–8 mm).

species_differences.leaf: Linear-lanceolate to narrowly ovate; truncate to weakly cordate

overlap_cautions: Male-flower counts and capsule sizes overlap; do not identify from one number alone.
Dark stem color is supporting evidence for T. nigricans, not proof.

FNA verifies T. brevispica staminate bracts 1–1.8 mm, persistent male pedicel bases 0.4–1.5 mm, and capsules 6.5–7 mm wide; pedicel bases and capsule widths overlap T. ramosa. Often only one capsule carpel matures, but this is not obligatory.
Do not handle stinging hairs barehanded.

FNA's strongest T. brevispica vs T. ramosa combination: often one mature carpel versus usually three; T. brevispica stigmas subpapillate to undulate and variable broad leaves, T. ramosa stigmas smooth to undulate and typically longer-than-wide narrower leaves. Stigma states overlap at undulate; fruit carpel condition is not obligatory.
lookalikes: Acalypha: pistillate bracts and divided styles rather than Tragia-style stinging racemes
Croton: stellate/scaly hairs and different inflorescence architecture
Euphorbia: cyathia instead of separate conventional unisexual flowers
Tragia urticifolia: compare persistent male pedicels and flower distribution
diagnostic_photo_checklist: Whole raceme, scale bar, female base and distal male flowers labeled
Matched leaf-base close-ups for all four species
Macro of persistent staminate pedicel bases with millimeter scale
Matched mature capsules with width scale
Whole-plant habit only as secondary context
Bract and pedicel detail of T. brevispica for diagnostic-review handoff
T. brevispica vs T. ramosa: matched stigmatic surface micro-macros, mature capsule showing 1 versus 3 developed carpels, and same-scale full leaf blades; provenance required before display.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: The entire flowering raceme, without touching the stinging hairs
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Find the lower pistillate flower(s), upper staminate flowers, bracts, and any remaining male-flower pedicel bases. Take a scaled side view.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: Mature leaf shape and leaf base, with ruler
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Compare triangular/cordate versus narrower blades; leaves alone cannot settle T. brevispica versus T. ramosa.

look_here_first_sequence.inspect: Male flower pedicel stubs and stigma surface, magnified
look_here_first_sequence.decision: Measure the persistent bases; note stigma smooth, undulate, or papillate, recognizing overlap.
Count developed carpels and measure capsule width; often one developed in T. brevispica versus usually three in T. ramosa, not an absolute rule.

shared_morphology_explained.caution: Handle using photographs or protection; stinging hairs alone do not identify the species.
Usually on the same raceme with female lower and male upper; photograph a complete reproductive axis.

shared_morphology_explained.plain: short flower stalk and the part left after the male flower falls
shared_morphology_explained.caution: The remnant length is measured in millimeters and overlaps between species.
Some species may mature fewer than three; count developed carpels on several ripe fruits.

anatomy_lessons.title: 1 · Read the raceme from bottom to top
anatomy_lessons.look_for: Lower female flowers or fruits and distal pollen-bearing flowers, including subtending bracts.
anatomy_lessons.why_it_matters: Shows that the green structures are separate unisexual flowers, not a Euphorbia cyathium.
anatomy_lessons.photo_role: complete intact raceme, side view, mm scale; compare four exact-species specimens

anatomy_lessons.title: 2 · Measure the fallen male-flower stalks
anatomy_lessons.look_for: Small pedicel remnants on the reproductive axis, with a 1-mm ruler; T. brevispica 0.4–1.5 mm and T. ramosa 0.4–1.5 mm overlap.
anatomy_lessons.why_it_matters: A useful structural measurement but NOT a stand-alone brevispica/ramosa separator.
anatomy_lessons.photo_role: paired male-flower stub macros of brevispica and ramosa at same scale

anatomy_lessons.title: 3 · Inspect the female stigma
anatomy_lessons.look_for: T. brevispica subpapillate-to-undulate versus T. ramosa smooth-to-undulate; undulate is shared.
anatomy_lessons.why_it_matters: Use in combination with leaf and fruit characters, not as a binary character.
anatomy_lessons.photo_role: paired side/top macro of pistillate flower with magnification

anatomy_lessons.title: 4 · Count the ripe fruit carpels
anatomy_lessons.look_for: T. brevispica often matures one of three carpels; T. ramosa usually three. Compare mature fruit widths (6.5–7 mm versus 6–8 mm, overlapping).
anatomy_lessons.why_it_matters: Carpel maturity is a stronger combined clue than fruit width alone, but not obligatory.
anatomy_lessons.photo_role: matched mature fruit faces and opened fruit with scale; one- versus three-developed-carpel examples

comparison_cards.title: T. brevispica vs T. ramosa — the hard pair
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Inspect leaf proportions, mature capsule carpel development, stigma texture and inflorescence together.
comparison_cards.key_contrast: T. brevispica 2–8(–10) staminate flowers and often one developed carpel; T. ramosa 2–20 flowers and usually three. Counts and sizes overlap.
comparison_cards.caution: Do not use 0.4–1.5 mm persistent pedicel bases or 6–8 mm capsules as binary splits.

comparison_cards.title: T. betonicifolia vs T. nigricans — leaf and raceme
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Compare triangular-ovate versus oblong/oblanceolate leaves, distribution of male flowers and measured stalk remnants.
comparison_cards.key_contrast: Betonicifolia tends to many distal male flowers and 0.3–0.6 mm bases; nigricans often 2–5 male flowers and 0.2–0.4 mm bases.
comparison_cards.caution: Leaf variation and measurement overlap require intact flowering racemes.

comparison_cards.title: Noseburn versus other spurges
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Confirm separate unisexual flowers in racemes; compare Acalypha female bracts, Croton hairs and Euphorbia cyathia.
comparison_cards.key_contrast: Stinging hairs + distinct male/female flowers + three-carpel capsule support Tragia; genus look-alikes require reproductive verification.
comparison_cards.caution: Do not identify from stinging sensation or leaf alone.
